newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Ariane "very far" from China rocket back-up deal.
newsitem.headline: Ariane "very far" from China rocket back-up deal.

text.p: Western Europe's satellite launch company Arianespace said on Monday it was far from an accord with Beijing to allow Europe's Ariane rocket to be used as a back-up in case of failure of China's Long March launcher, space officials said.
"There has been no agreement signed with Long March," Arianespace president told a space conference here.

The French newspaper Le Monde said on Saturday that France's minister for post, telecommunications and space, Francois Fillon, would raise the issue on an official visit to China that started on Sunday. Fillon is being accompanied by Arianespace director general Francis Avanzi.
The report said the aim was not to transfer valuable European space technology nor help China develop its rockets, but to make Arianespace more competitive.

"Mr. Fillon clearly stated that his trip to China contained a certain number of objectives and among these objectives -- his staff went so far as to say -- that an objective for an accord between Long March and Ariane was not a bad idea to consider ... We are very far from signing such an agreement," Bigot added.

The Paris-based firm that controls more than half the world's commercial rocket market fears its lead is threatened by American consolidation -- notably the planned purchase of McDonnell Douglas Corp by Boeing.
Arianespace launches the Ariane-4 rocket series from the European Space Agency (ESA) launch center in Kourou, French Guiana, on the northeast coast of South America.

It successfully launched 15 satellites aboard 10 Ariane-4 rockets in 1996 and signed firm contracts during the year for the launch of 19 more satellites, which brings its "firm" satellite launch orders to 42, worth an estimated $3.5 billion. Bigot said serious options brought the total number of satellite launch contracts to 55.
But on June 4, the first new generation Ariane-5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after its maiden launch in a major setback for the European space program.

Arianespace was scheduled to take over commercial operations of Ariane-5 early this year -- but the new rocket's commercial future is now in doubt and a second experimental launch of the more powerful rocket is now planned for July at earliest.
The China Great Wall Industry Corp launches commercial satellites on its Long March rocket. The Long March has been hit by a spate of spectacular accidents in the last two years.
Last Aug. 18, a Long March 3 rocket failed to put into proper orbit the U.S.-made Chinasat-7 telecommunications satellite.
Last February, a Long March 3B rocket exploded a few seconds after liftoff, killing six people.
In January 1995, six people were killed when a Long March launcher carrying an Apstar 2 satellite blew up.

Boeing's planned purchase of McDonnell Douglas will give the new company a slice of the Sea Launch satellite system being prepared for its maiden flight in 1998 using a Russian Zenit rocket launched from an offshore drilling platform in the Pacific Ocean. Boeing has a 40 percent stake in the project.
It will also hand it McDonnell Douglas' flight-proven Delta family of rockets, used to launch satellites from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Lockheed Martin controls the International Launch Services (ILS) company that launches the Atlas and Russia's Proton rocket.
Specialists said major satellite launch companies had underestimated the demand for their services in the early 1990s, particularly from booming markets in the Asia-Pacific region.
